title: The title word
hookLine: after the Mool Mantar comes one word, jap: recite, repeat, remember

lines: A STICKY NOTE ON THE MIRROR.
ONE WORD, ON ITS OWN LINE.
cards: One word on a sticky note on the bathroom mirror: call. Milk. Breathe.

Not a sentence, because one word is all you need to remember by. Right after the Mool Mantar, before the first verse of Japji begins, a single word stands on its own line. Most people read straight past it.
It's the title of the whole hymn. And it isn't really a name, the way a book title is. It's closer to a note on the mirror.

teach.b: The word is jap. In Gurmukhi it's just two letters, with a small vowel mark under the second that carries grammar and is mostly left silent.
You've met its meaning before, folded inside a longer name: on day twenty-one and again on day one hundred twenty-nine, Japji Sahib, the recitation, with ji and sahib added for respect.
Today, look at the word with the respect taken off, standing alone on its line. Across Indian religious life there's a practice called japa: repeating a sacred name or phrase, often on beads.
You met the mala in camp three. Jap comes from the same root.
So the bare title of Guru Nanak's great morning hymn reads like one instruction: repeat.

teach.h: THE TITLE, WITH THE RESPECT TAKEN OFF.
teach.b: Or: remember. But Japji itself will teach that it isn't asking for mechanical repetition.

Much later in the hymn, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that if one tongue became a hundred thousand, and each repeated the Name a hundred thousand times, those would be the steps of a stairway toward the Lord.

Repetition is a stairway. Yet the whole hymn insists the point is remembering, not counting: keeping the One in mind while you live. That's why jap sits so close to simran, remembrance, from camp three.

Say something enough times and it stops being something you say and becomes something you know in your bones, like your own phone number, a friend's laugh, the way home in the dark. Jap asks for that kind of knowing.
The stairway is made of small repetitions. Each one is only one step.

how: Japji Sahib takes its name from jap, to recite and remember; Sikhs recite it each morning, and many also repeat Waheguru or the Mool Mantar through the day as simran.

o: to read a text closely to grasp its meaning
to pray silently for something you want
to recite and remember, again and again

games.q: Guru Nanak pictures one tongue becoming a hundred thousand, each repeating the Name a hundred thousand times. what does he call that?
o: the steps of a stairway toward the Lord.
a rule every Sikh must count.
games.why: later in Japji, the repetitions are the steps of a stairway; each is only one step.

practice: On your next out-breath, whisper the word jap, then breathe in, three times over.
Then stop and listen to the quiet after it, the way a room sounds after a bell, and notice what you'd like to remember today: a person, a promise, the One, if that's your language.
If you pray, let Waheguru follow on the next breaths, and rest there.

wordCard.voice: Jap. Recite, repeat, remember: the one-word title of Guru Nanak's morning hymn.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jap, the title of Japji. the small mark under the last letter is grammar, mostly silent.

carryVoice: Your line: repeat, remember. One word stood alone at the top of Japji today. A hundred and sixty days now.
